title: Problems involving percentages
summary: Model multi-step percentage problems involving profit, loss, discounts, taxes, budgets and mixtures while tracking the reference quantity at each step.
objectives: Translate a percentage problem into quantities, reference bases and multipliers.
Solve multi-step applications involving money, budgets and mixtures.
Verify a solution using estimation, units and a forward calculation.

sections.title: Label the base at every step

blocks.text: Many errors come from using the correct percentage with the wrong base. Mark the quantity that represents 100% at each stage. Profit percentage commonly uses cost price as its base; discount uses marked price; tax is calculated on the price after any discount.

sections.title: Build the calculation before evaluating it

blocks.text: Write each increase or decrease as a multiplier and keep exact values until the last step. For mixtures or budgets, translate each statement separately, then combine the resulting amounts. Finally check that the units and size of the answer fit the context.

Cost price is what a seller pays for an item; selling price is what the customer pays. Profit = selling price − cost price, and profit percentage uses the cost price as the base. The marked price is the price shown before any discount; a discount is a percentage of the marked price. A mark-up is a percentage added to the cost price to set the marked price.

Commission is a percentage of the value of sales paid to the person who made them. A sales tax, such as Singapore’s Goods and Services Tax (GST, 9%), is a percentage added to the price after any discount. Simple interest on a sum P at R% per year for T years is
For example, S$2000 at 3% per year for 4 years earns 2000 × 3 × 4 ÷ 100 = S$240 interest.

sections.title: Worked example: percentages of a budget

prompt.text: A club spends 35% of a S$2400 budget on equipment and 25% of the remainder on transport. How much remains?

content.text: After equipment, 65% of the budget remains.
After transport, 75% of that remainder is left.

sections.verification_note: S$1170 is 48.75% of the original budget, matching the combined multiplier 0.65 × 0.75 = 0.4875.

sections.title: Worked example: mark-up, discount and profit

prompt.text: A shop buys a bag for S$80 and marks it up by 40%. It then sells the bag at a 15% discount on the marked price. Find the selling price and the profit as a percentage of the cost price.

content.text: Mark-up: the marked price is 140% of the cost price.
Discount: the selling price is 85% of the marked price.
The profit is S$95.20 − S$80 = S$15.20. Use the cost price as the base.

sections.verification_note: The overall multiplier is 1.40 × 0.85 = 1.19, which is a 19% profit, matching the answer.

sections.title: Worked example: change a concentration

prompt.text: A 500 ml drink is 30% juice. How much water must be added so that juice is 20% of the final drink?

content.text: Find the fixed amount of juice.
Let the final volume be V. The 150 ml of juice is 20% of V.

sections.verification_note: After adding 250 ml of water, 150/750 = 0.20, so the final drink is 20% juice.

prompt.text: An item costs S$200 and sells for S$230. Find the profit as a percentage of the cost price.

feedback.text: The profit is S$30. Cost price is the reference, so 30 ÷ 200 × 100% = 15%.

blocks.text: Name the 100% base for every percentage, translate changes into multipliers, preserve exact values through the working, and verify the final result against the wording, units and a reasonable estimate.
